title: GSP 202 Continuous Assessment (CA) Workbook — Official Solutions & Study Guide

chapters.chapter_title: The State, Conflict Resolution, and Development in Africa

questions.question: The State is synonymous with such other concepts as ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Country, Nation, and Government
questions.notes: Often used interchangeably in everyday political discourse, though technically distinct political and sociological concepts.

questions.question: The concept, nature and functions of state have undergone considerable changes due to numerous ________.
questions.answer: socio-political and economic transformations (and competing philosophical traditions)
questions.notes: From ancient city-states to Westphalian nation-states and modern post-colonial states.

questions.question: According to R. M. MacIver (1926), the State performs the special function of maintaining social order through an agency called ________.
questions.answer: Government
questions.notes: Government is the administrative apparatus/machinery through which the state's will is formulated and executed.

questions.question: ________ defined the state as 'a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory'.
questions.answer: Max Weber (1919)
questions.notes: Foundational sociological definition of the modern state in 'Politics as a Vocation'.

questions.question: ________ in his book titled ________ expressed the idea of the state as 'the power which has authority over men'.
questions.answer: Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince (1513)
questions.notes: Machiavelli decoupled political statecraft from classical theological morality.

questions.question: According to Locke, the three natural rights that are encapsulated in the principles of liberalism are ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Life, Liberty, and Property (Estate)
questions.notes: John Locke argued governments exist solely to protect these inalienable natural rights under social contract.

questions.question: ________ refers to the entities that operate independently of the state and serve as platform for individuals to express their views, engage in collective action, and hold the state accountable.
questions.answer: Civil Society (NGOs, community unions, professional bodies)
questions.notes: Acts as a watchdog and intermediary between citizens and state institutions.

questions.question: According to the Liberals, the system of checks and balances ensures that power is shared among the three arms of government namely ________, ________, and ________ to check abuse of power.
questions.answer: Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary
questions.notes: Doctrine of Separation of Powers formulated by Baron de Montesquieu (1748).

questions.question: ________ viewed the state as a tool used by the ruling class to suppress the working class and prevent them from achieving class consciousness.
questions.answer: Karl Marx / Marxism
questions.notes: The Communist Manifesto: 'The executive of the modern state is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie.'

questions.question: Africa as a continent was partitioned by Colonial powers in a German city called ________ in the year ________.
questions.answer: Berlin, 1884–1885 (Berlin West Africa Conference)
questions.notes: Convened by Otto von Bismarck; partitioned Africa into arbitrary colonial borders without African representation.

questions.question: The inevitable class struggle that will lead to the eventual overthrow of the ruling class by the exploited class to achieve a more just and equitable society is called ________.
questions.answer: Proletarian / Socialist Revolution
questions.notes: Marxist historical materialism predicting the rise of a classless, stateless communist society.

questions.question: The exclusive authority and autonomy of a state to govern itself without external interference is called ________. It was established as international law through the ________ in the year ________.
questions.answer: Sovereignty; Treaty of Westphalia; 1648
questions.notes: The 1648 Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War and instituted modern sovereign statehood.

questions.question: Sovereignty has two dimensions namely ________ and ________.
questions.answer: Internal Sovereignty and External Sovereignty
questions.notes: Internal: supreme legal authority over subjects within borders. External: independence from foreign overlordship and international recognition.

questions.question: According to Loshkariov (2024), the sovereignty of African States have been constrained by a number of factors including ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Weak institutional capacity, economic dependency/foreign debt, and external geopolitical interference / porous borders
questions.notes: Limits the empirical capacity of post-colonial African states to exercise total sovereign control.

questions.question: In the Middle Belt, farmer-herder clashes are exacerbated by ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Climate change/desertification, resource competition (land and water), and ethnic/religious polarization
questions.notes: Migration of pastoralists southward into agrarian host communities sparks violent resource clashes.

questions.question: The Nigerian civil war lasted from ________ to ________.
questions.answer: 6th July 1967 to 15th January 1970
questions.notes: Sparked by the secession of the Republic of Biafra following pogroms and breakdown of the Aburi Accord.

questions.question: The major achievement of the South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) is ________.
questions.answer: Fostering restorative justice, public confession, and national healing without plunging into retributive vengeance
questions.notes: Chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu under President Nelson Mandela after the fall of apartheid.

questions.question: The two major classes in every society identified by Karl Marx who are ever embroiled in antagonistic relationship are ________ and ________.
questions.answer: The Bourgeoisie (owners of capital/means of production) and the Proletariat (wage labourers)
questions.notes: Fundamental dichotomy of industrial capitalist social structure in Marxist sociology.

questions.question: What is class consciousness?
questions.answer: The self-awareness of a social class regarding its collective economic interests, systemic exploitation, and political power to organize and transform society.
questions.notes: Transition from a 'class-in-itself' (objective grouping) to a 'class-for-itself' (politically conscious actors).

questions.question: According to Karl Marx, what is the major disadvantage of the laissez-faire and free market economy?
questions.answer: Widening inequality, exploitation of the working class, and the alienation of labour (estrangement from product, process, self, and fellow workers).
questions.notes: Capitalists extract surplus value from workers' unpaid labor to accumulate private wealth.

questions.question: The liberal philosophy is based on the principles of ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Individual liberty, the rule of law, consent of the governed, private property rights, and free market competition
questions.notes: Champions limited government, human rights, and institutional constitutionalism.

questions.question: The state, acting as a primary mediator and arbiter in conflict resolution, uses the following three mechanisms namely ________, ________, and ________ to manage violence and promote stability.
questions.answer: Judicial adjudication (courts), Administrative negotiation/mediation (commissions of inquiry), and Law enforcement / coercive peacekeeping (police and military)
questions.notes: The state's institutional tools to deter violence and enforce binding conflict settlements.

questions.question: According to the former UN Secretary-General, Kofi Annan, ________, ________, and ________ make up the building blocks of human and national security.
questions.answer: Peace, Development, and Human Rights
questions.notes: 'We will not enjoy development without security, we will not enjoy security without development, and we will not enjoy either without respect for human rights.'

questions.question: The 1994 UNDP landmark report on human security identified the characteristics of human security namely ________, ________, ________, and ________. And factors hindering Nigeria's fight against terrorism include ________ and ________.
questions.answer: Characteristics: Universal, People-centred, Interdependent, and Early prevention. Terror hindering factors: Corruption, porous borders, and weak state intelligence coordination.
questions.notes: Shifted security paradigm from state territory defense to human dignity, safety, and freedom from want/fear.

chapters.chapter_title: Ethnic and Communal Conflicts in Africa

questions.question: ________ refers to the use of a people's collective identity to successfully get more than their fair share of the social benefit in society.
questions.answer: Ethnicity / Ethnic Politics
questions.notes: Ethnicity is politicized when collective identity is weaponized to gain competitive advantages in resource allocation.

questions.question: ________ is a community of people who possess a common identity based on common origin, kinship ties, historical experiences, traditions, cultures, and language.
questions.answer: Ethnic Group
questions.notes: A distinct sociological group sharing common cultural symbols and ancestral heritage.

questions.question: According to Ojiezele & Ojo (2024), the social phenomenon that drives the dynamics in society and which traverses the entire spectrum of African life, including human identity and social organization is called ________.
questions.answer: Ethnicity
questions.notes: Ethnicity profoundly shapes social stratification and political patronage in contemporary Africa.

questions.question: The major theories of ethnicity are ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Primordialism, Instrumentalism, and Constructivism
questions.notes: Three prominent theoretical paradigms explaining ethnic attachment and mobilization.

questions.question: Briefly explain the theories of ethnicity: (i) Primordialism, (ii) Instrumentalism, (iii) Constructivism.
questions.answer: (i) Primordialism: Views ethnic identity as deeply innate, fixed, and biological based on ancient ancestry and language. (ii) Instrumentalism: Views ethnicity as an instrument or elite political tool manipulated to capture political power and state resources. (iii) Constructivism: Views ethnicity as a dynamic, socially constructed identity shaped by historical context and social interactions.
questions.notes: Fundamental theoretical division in ethnic studies and conflict sociology.

questions.question: The use of local chiefs by the colonial power to access and control resources through patronizing relationship and reward for loyalty is called ________.
questions.answer: Indirect Rule (and the Warrant Chief System)
questions.notes: Introduced by Lord Frederick Lugard; entrenched divide-and-rule governance across Nigeria.

questions.question: According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI, 2022), the major causes of conflict among the major ethnic groups in Nigeria are ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Political marginalization, competition for scarce economic resources, and historical mutual distrust/cultural antagonism
questions.notes: Structural grievances combined with perceived domination and demographic pressure.

questions.question: The three major examples of protracted ethnic-related conflicts in Nigeria are ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Ife-Modakeke conflict (Osun State), Aguleri-Umuleri conflict (Anambra State), and Tiv-Jukun conflict (Taraba/Benue State)
questions.notes: Historic disputes over land ownership, chieftaincy authority, and political representation.

questions.question: In the Congo Democratic Republic (DRC), the major ethnic groups that fought over resources are ________ and ________.
questions.answer: Hema (pastoralists) and Lendu (agriculturalists)
questions.notes: The Ituri conflict over control of land, gold mines, and cross-border trade.

questions.question: ________ (2010) argued that ethnicity is not the driving force of African conflicts but a lever used by politicians to mobilize supporters in pursuit of ________ and ________.
questions.answer: Paul Collier (or Posner); political power and economic resources (wealth)
questions.notes: Instrumentalist argument highlighting elite greed rather than ancient tribal hatred.

questions.question: Social identity groups and entities coexisted peacefully in Africa as aggregates with a high degree of interrelationship which is reinforced through ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Intermarriage, trade networks / commercial partnerships, and shared religious / cultural celebrations
questions.notes: Pre-colonial African social systems frequently exhibited integrative inter-communal linkages.

questions.question: The two major ethnic groups involved in the 1994 Rwanda genocide are ________ and ________.
questions.answer: Hutus and Tutsis
questions.notes: Over 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were slaughtered in 100 days.

questions.question: Name the violent groups that are implicated in the inter-ethnic conflicts in the following regions in Nigeria: (i) North-West, (ii) North-East, (iii) Middle Belt.
questions.answer: (i) North-West: Armed Bandits / Cattle Rustlers / Yan Sakai vigilantes; (ii) North-East: Boko Haram (JAS) and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP); (iii) Middle Belt: Armed Pastoralist Militias and Ethnic Farmer Self-defense groups.
questions.notes: Regional security dynamics combining ideological extremism with resource banditry.

questions.question: According to Call (2003), Africans can build unified nations with many ethnicities living and coexisting peacefully by taking the following steps: ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Building inclusive state institutions, ensuring equitable resource distribution, and entrenching the rule of law with constitutional protections for minority rights
questions.notes: Peacebuilding strategies aimed at neutralizing ethnic zero-sum games.

questions.question: If 'Democracy means much more than elections' then Democracy as remedy for social conflicts in Africa must connote the following attributes: ________.
questions.answer: Constitutionalism, protection of human rights and minority interests, transparent accountability, judicial independence, and participatory governance
questions.notes: Substantive democracy beyond mere periodic electoral rituals.

questions.question: Briefly explain the three types of ethnic identity conflict outlined by Okonkwo (2025): ________.
questions.answer: (i) Majority-Minority Hegemony conflict (where a demographic majority dominates state apparatus); (ii) Indigene-Settler dichotomy conflict (where citizenship and resource rights depend on ancestral land origins); (iii) Boundary/Territorial demarcation conflict (disputes over communal borders and natural wealth).
questions.notes: Typology of ethnic structural friction in modern multi-ethnic polities.

questions.question: Explain with relevant examples the following types of ethnic identity conflicts identified by Irobi (2005): (i) Ethno-nationalist conflicts, (ii) Ethnic rivalry conflicts, (iii) Ethno-religious conflicts, (iv) Resource-based conflicts, (v) Identity-based conflicts.
questions.answer: (i) Ethno-nationalist: Self-determination or secession demands (e.g. Biafra / Nigerian Civil War); (ii) Ethnic rivalry: Struggle for national dominance between major ethnic groups (e.g. Hausa-Yoruba-Igbo political rivalry); (iii) Ethno-religious: Ethnic clashes overlapping with religious divide (e.g. Jos / Kaduna riots); (iv) Resource-based: Competition over land, water or minerals (e.g. Niger Delta oil, Tiv-Jukun land); (v) Identity-based: Struggles over communal dignity and recognition (e.g. Ife-Modakeke).
questions.notes: Comprehensive taxonomy of identity-driven crises.

chapters.chapter_title: Climate Change, Resource Conflict and Environmental Security

questions.question: ________ is defined as the prevailing state of the climate on all temporal and spatial scales beyond that of individual weather events.
questions.answer: Climate
questions.notes: Statistical description of weather parameters over periods ranging from months to thousands of years.

questions.question: Changes in the average state of the atmosphere over time can be brought about by such processes as ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Natural internal variability, volcanic eruptions / solar cycles, and human (anthropogenic) activities
questions.notes: Natural and anthropogenic climate forcing mechanisms.

questions.question: The large-scale modifications of the land surface and atmospheric composition of greenhouse gases is chiefly attributed to ________.
questions.answer: Anthropogenic (Human) activities (such as industrialization, fossil fuel combustion, and extensive deforestation)
questions.notes: Human-induced disruption of the global carbon cycle.

questions.question: ________ refers to the measurable increase in the earth's average temperature caused by rising concentrations of greenhouse gases.
questions.answer: Global Warming
questions.notes: Average surface temperature increase driving climate destabilization.

questions.question: One negative consequence of the industrial revolution is ________.
questions.answer: Massive atmospheric carbon emissions, widespread environmental degradation, and accelerated global warming
questions.notes: Shift to fossil fuels initiated unprecedented greenhouse gas accumulation.

questions.question: The phrase 'heat-trapping blanket' refers to ________.
questions.answer: The layer of greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, water vapor) in the troposphere that traps infrared thermal radiation escaping the earth surface
questions.notes: Natural thermal regulation turned into severe warming by excessive emissions.

questions.question: What does the term 'the greenhouse effect' mean?
questions.answer: A natural planetary process where atmospheric gases absorb and re-radiate infrared heat back toward Earth, keeping the biosphere warm enough to sustain life.
questions.notes: Distinction between the essential natural greenhouse effect and the enhanced anthropogenic greenhouse effect.

questions.question: What is Coastal Development?
questions.answer: Human alteration of shorelines and coastal zones through urbanization, construction of ports, resorts, land reclamation, and industrial facilities.
questions.notes: Urban expansion in sensitive littoral ecosystems.

questions.question: What are the human activities involved in coastal development?
questions.answer: Sand dredging, mangrove deforestation, building of maritime infrastructure, discharge of untreated industrial effluents, and coastal land reclamation.
questions.notes: Destroys natural shoreline buffers and increases vulnerability to tidal surges.

questions.question: How does coastal development drive climate change?
questions.answer: By destroying mangrove forests and coastal wetlands (which are super-efficient carbon sinks) and releasing sequestered 'blue carbon' into the atmosphere.
questions.notes: Mangroves sequester up to 4 times more carbon per hectare than terrestrial rainforests.

questions.question: What is Deforestation?
questions.answer: The permanent removal or clear-cutting of standing forest lands for agriculture, logging, urbanization, or mining without reforestation.
questions.notes: Major driver of biodiversity loss and terrestrial carbon emissions.

questions.question: How does Deforestation bring about climate change?
questions.answer: Trees absorb CO2; cutting or burning them eliminates active carbon sinks and releases their stored carbon dioxide directly into the atmosphere.
questions.notes: Responsible for approximately 10-15% of all global greenhouse gas emissions.

questions.question: What is an urban heat island?
questions.answer: An urban or metropolitan area that experiences significantly warmer temperatures than surrounding rural areas due to human activities, dense concrete, and asphalt.
questions.notes: Microclimate anomaly caused by dense built environments and vehicular exhaust.

questions.question: What causes urban heat island?
questions.answer: Replacement of natural vegetation with heat-absorbing concrete and asphalt, waste heat from air conditioners and engines, and tall buildings blocking wind flow.
questions.notes: Dark surfaces retain thermal energy during daytime and radiate it at night.

questions.question: What are the consequences of an urban heat island?
questions.answer: Increased energy consumption for cooling, elevated air pollution and smog, heat exhaustion / cardiovascular stress, and increased urban heat mortality.
questions.notes: Severe public health impacts on vulnerable elderly and low-income populations.

questions.question: How does the burning of fossil fuels aggravate climate change?
questions.answer: Combustion of coal, petroleum, and natural gas chemically combines carbon with oxygen, releasing millions of metric tonnes of CO2 that trap thermal radiation in the atmosphere.
questions.notes: The primary anthropogenic contributor to global temperature rise.

questions.question: What are the primary greenhouse gases in Earth's atmosphere?
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide (CO2), Methane (CH4), Nitrous oxide (N2O), Water vapor (H2O), and Ozone (O3)
questions.notes: Methane has a warming potential over 28 times higher than CO2 over a 100-year timescale.

questions.question: Briefly explain the impact of climate change under: (i) Threat to biodiversity, (ii) Sea level rise, (iii) Flooding and changes in weather patterns, (iv) Diseases and health challenges.
questions.answer: (i) Biodiversity: Habitat loss, coral bleaching, and species extinction. (ii) Sea level rise: Thermal water expansion and melting glaciers threatening coastal cities. (iii) Weather extremes: Unprecedented droughts, torrential deluges, and irregular rainfall. (iv) Health challenges: Proliferation of vector-borne diseases (malaria, dengue) and heatstroke.
questions.notes: Systemic ecological and humanitarian impacts.

questions.question: Why is it said that climate change acts as a 'threat multiplier'?
questions.answer: Because it does not create conflicts in isolation, but compounds existing poverty, governance deficits, resource scarcity, and ethnic frictions into violent crises.
questions.notes: Drives pastoralist migrations from the arid Sahel into farming communities in Central and Southern Nigeria.

questions.question: The physical and biological surroundings within a specific area or context is called ________.
questions.answer: Environment
questions.notes: Includes biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) elements interacting in ecosystems.

questions.question: Name and briefly explain the two primary components of the environment.
questions.answer: (i) Biotic component: All living organisms including humans, animals, plants, and microorganisms; (ii) Abiotic component: All non-living physical elements including air, water, soil, minerals, sunlight, and climate.
questions.notes: Ecological foundation of life-support systems.

questions.question: The confidence or guarantee that individuals and communities will continue to have access to the essential conditions and resources necessary for human survival and overall wellbeing is called ________.
questions.answer: Environmental Security
questions.notes: Shifts security thinking from state military defense to preserving natural resource sustainability.

chapters.chapter_title: Technology and Digital Threats to Peace and Security

questions.question: Explain each of the following in a short sentence: (i) Artificial Intelligence (AI), (ii) Internet of Things (IoT), (iii) Biotechnology, (iv) Autonomous Weapon Systems (AWS), (v) Cybersecurity.
questions.answer: (i) AI: Machines simulated to perform tasks requiring human intelligence like reasoning, perception, and learning. (ii) IoT: Interconnected network of physical devices embedded with sensors to collect and exchange data. (iii) Biotechnology: Exploitation of biological organisms or systems for industrial, medical, and agricultural processes. (iv) AWS: Weapons that independently select and engage targets without human intervention. (v) Cybersecurity: Safeguarding computer networks, devices, and digital systems from illicit attacks, theft, or damage.
questions.notes: Core Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) technological pillars.

questions.question: ________ refers to the protection of individuals and communities from harms caused by the misuse of digital technologies, that threaten peace, stability, trust, and well-being.
questions.answer: Digital Human Security
questions.notes: Shields citizens against algorithmic discrimination, surveillance capitalism, and online harassment.

questions.question: ________ refers to the protection of countries and the international system from digital threats that can disrupt stability, sovereignty, and peace.
questions.answer: Cybersecurity / National Cyber Defense
questions.notes: Guards critical national infrastructure (power, telecommunications, banking) against hostile state and non-state actors.

questions.question: Explain briefly why technology is considered a 'double-edged sword'.
questions.answer: While technology drives extraordinary medical, educational, and communication advances for human progress, it simultaneously provides potent tools for cyber warfare, state surveillance, disinformation, and automated lethal destruction.
questions.notes: Dual-use nature of emerging technological paradigms.

questions.question: Digital technology contributes to direct violence through ________.
questions.answer: Autonomous weapon systems (killer robots), armed drones, precision cyber-sabotage of hospital/energy grids, and online recruitment for terrorist violence
questions.notes: Direct kinetic and fatal consequences facilitated by algorithmic and digital networks.

questions.question: Structural violence emerges when ________ marginalize populations.
questions.answer: Algorithmic biases, surveillance states, and unequal digital access (the digital divide)
questions.notes: Systemic inequalities codified into technological architectures.

questions.question: Misinformation, deepfakes, and information disorder pose threats to peace and security by ________.
questions.answer: Eroding public trust in institutions, inciting ethnic and religious violence, manipulating electoral outcomes, and distorting objective factual reality
questions.notes: Weaponization of generative AI and synthetic media to trigger mass civil unrest.

questions.question: Excessive monitoring with the use of digital surveillance can undermine peace through ________.
questions.answer: Stifling democratic dissent, violating citizens' constitutional privacy rights, intimidating civil society activists, and enabling authoritarian repression
questions.notes: Digital authoritarianism through spyware (e.g. Pegasus) and ubiquitous facial recognition.

questions.question: Positive uses of Technology as a tool for peacebuilding include ________.
questions.answer: Conflict early warning systems, crowdsourced crisis mapping, inclusive digital peace dialogues, verification of human rights violations, and educational dissemination
questions.notes: PeaceTech applications empowering grassroots communities and humanitarian responders.

questions.question: According to Russell & Norvig (2020), Artificial Intelligence refers to systems capable of performing tasks that normally require human intelligence such as ________.
questions.answer: Visual perception, speech recognition, decision-making under uncertainty, and natural language translation
questions.notes: Standard computational definition from leading AI scholars.

questions.question: Artificial Intelligence systems include ________.
questions.answer: Machine learning algorithms, deep neural networks, computer vision systems, natural language processing models, and expert decision-support systems
questions.notes: Key subfields of current artificial intelligence architecture.

questions.question: Artificial Intelligence can enhance peace and security by ________.
questions.answer: Automating threat detection, predicting conflict outbreaks through sentiment analysis, monitoring border security, and identifying illicit arms trafficking
questions.notes: Predictive analytics deployed for early intervention and humanitarian protection.

questions.question: Artificial Intelligence also poses significant digital threats through Autonomous weapon systems that can be misused in ________.
questions.answer: Targeted assassinations, indiscriminate warfare without human empathy or moral judgment, and algorithmic warfare lowering the threshold for armed conflict
questions.notes: Legal and ethical accountability vacuum under International Humanitarian Law (Geneva Conventions).

questions.question: The acronym LAWS stands for ________ and it can independently do ________.
questions.answer: Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems; search for, identify, track, and engage (kill) targets without human command or oversight
questions.notes: Colloquially known as 'killer robots' subject to UN disarmament debates.

questions.question: Artificial intelligence (AI) poses threat to peace and security through ________.
questions.answer: Autonomous cyberattacks, automated generation of scalable propaganda/deepfakes, and algorithmic entrenchment of societal biases and systemic discrimination
questions.notes: Low cost and high velocity of automated malicious operations.

questions.question: ________ across cultures, time, and space have been subjected to varying degrees of ill-treatment in one way or another.
questions.answer: Women (and girls)
questions.notes: Historical universality of gender-based discrimination.

questions.question: ________ is a kind of conflict that arises from deprivation, subjugation, denial of rights, unjust treatments, and punishments inflicted on a person or a people basically because of their gender.
questions.answer: Gender-Based Violence (GBV) / Gender Conflict
questions.notes: Harm inflicted that is rooted in structural gender inequalities and discriminatory social expectations.

questions.question: Oftentimes, ________ is perpetrated by men in the expression of their self-acclaimed superiority and protection of their ego and interests.
questions.answer: Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) / Domestic Violence / Patriarchal Aggression
questions.notes: Patriarchal entitlement driving interpersonal violence against women.

questions.question: International instruments aimed at combating gender-based violence include United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325, the Beijing Platform for Action (1995), and the 1993 Declaration on the ________.
questions.answer: Elimination of Violence Against Women (DEVAW)
questions.notes: Key milestone global human rights frameworks safeguarding women.

questions.question: The concept of gender is usually and incorrectly used interchangeably with ________.
questions.answer: Sex (Biological Sex)
questions.notes: Crucial sociological distinction: sex is biological; gender is socio-culturally constructed.

questions.question: While sex refers to the biological and physiological characteristics that define males and females, gender is a ________.
questions.answer: Social construct (socially learned roles, behaviours, attributes, and identities considered appropriate for men and women)
questions.notes: Gender expectations vary across cultures and evolve over historical time.

questions.question: The acronym OSAGI stands for the ________.
questions.answer: Office of the Special Adviser on Gender Issues and Advancement of Women
questions.notes: United Nations specialized agency established to spearhead gender mainstreaming.

questions.question: The World Health Organization (2023) states that gender intersects with social and economic inequalities through the framework of ________.
questions.answer: Intersectionality
questions.notes: Kimberle Crenshaw's concept showing how gender overlaps with class, race, disability, and age.

questions.question: ________ implies that gender is relational?
questions.answer: Gender Relationality (meaning gender roles cannot be understood in isolation, but only in how femininity and masculinity are defined in relation to each other)
questions.notes: Masculine privileges are directly tied to the subordination of feminine counterparts.

questions.question: Pre-colonial African societies exhibited diverse patterns of gendered ________.
questions.answer: Complementarity and female political leadership (e.g. Queen Amina of Zazzau, Iyalode in Yorubaland, Omu in Igboland)
questions.notes: Demonstrates that absolute female subjugation was not uniform across ancestral Africa.

questions.question: ________ theoretical perspectives help illuminate how the existence of patriarchal hierarchies provides a structural basis for the subordination of women and the regulation of female behaviour.
questions.answer: Feminist and Radical Feminist
questions.notes: Focuses on patriarchy as an institutionalized system of male domination.

questions.question: ________ significantly reshaped gender relations, reinforcing male dominance while disrupting pre-existing social systems.
questions.answer: Colonialism (European Colonial Rule / Victorian Patriarchy)
questions.notes: Colonial taxation and Warrant Chief systems disenfranchised traditional African women leaders.

questions.question: ________ theory can help explain how these colonial interventions normalized hierarchical gender relations.
questions.answer: Post-Colonial Feminist / Decolonial
questions.notes: Examines how European colonial administrators imposed Western patriarchal gender binaries onto African societies.

questions.question: ________ in Liberia, Sierra Leone, and the Democratic Republic of Congo provide stark examples of how historical inequalities and disrupted social structures amplify violence against women.
questions.answer: Armed Civil Wars and Resource Conflicts
questions.notes: Widespread collapse of civil protection systems leading to systemic sexual violence.

questions.question: ________ have used sexual violence strategically to intimidate populations, control communities, and reinforce power hierarchies.
questions.answer: Armed Combatants, Rebel Militias, and Military Formations
questions.notes: Sexual violence utilized as a deliberate weapon and tactic of war.

questions.question: Feminist theory has been central to scholarly discussions on GBV, emphasizing the structural underpinnings of violence within ________ societies.
questions.answer: Patriarchal
questions.notes: Attributes violence to power imbalances rather than isolated individual pathology.

questions.question: The concept of ________ demonstrates that dominant forms of masculinity legitimize aggression and control as markers of male authority.
questions.answer: Hegemonic Masculinity (R. W. Connell)
questions.notes: Cultural archetype that equates true manhood with physical toughness and subjugation of women.

questions.question: ________ theory provides insight into the behavioural transmission of violence.
questions.answer: Social Learning Theory (Albert Bandura)
questions.notes: Explains how aggressive behavior is acquired through social observation and modeling.

questions.question: Bandura (1977) proposed that behaviour, including violent behaviour, is learned through observation, imitation, and ________.
questions.answer: Modeling (and Vicarious Reinforcement)
questions.notes: Cognitive-behavioral acquisition of interpersonal violence.

questions.question: The belief that exposure to domestic violence during formative years significantly increases the likelihood of becoming a perpetrator or a victim in adulthood demonstrates the ________ nature of GBV.
questions.answer: Intergenerational (Cycle of Violence)
questions.notes: Transmission of learned abusive behavior across familial generations.

questions.question: ________ theory situates GBV within multi-level contexts, recognizing that violence emerges from the interaction of individual, relational, community, and societal factors.
questions.answer: Ecological (Socio-Ecological Framework)
questions.notes: Pioneered by Lori Heise and adopted by WHO to analyze nested drivers of violence.

questions.question: ________ holds that intimate partner violence is not a spontaneous expression of anger but a deliberate strategy to assert and maintain control.
questions.answer: Power and Control Theory (Feminist Interpersonal Model)
questions.notes: Visualized through the Duluth Power and Control Wheel.

questions.question: Cultural and normative theories elucidate the role of social values, traditions, and ________ in perpetuating GBV.
questions.answer: Customary norms / Cultural taboos
questions.notes: Community justifications that normalize domestic abuse and victim blaming.

questions.question: ________ theory underscores the importance of socioeconomic interventions, including women's economic empowerment and poverty reduction, in mitigating GBV.
questions.answer: Structural / Feminist Political Economy
questions.notes: Financial dependence leaves women trapped in abusive marriages.

questions.question: ________ perspectives emphasize how personality traits, emotional regulation, and trauma history contribute to violent behaviours.
questions.answer: Psychological and Psychopathological
questions.notes: Explores individual clinical factors, substance abuse, and impulse control deficits.

questions.question: The ________ approach has been pivotal in promoting legal frameworks and international advocacy for GBV prevention.
questions.answer: Human Rights-Based
questions.notes: Frames GBV as an egregious violation of basic fundamental human rights.

questions.question: Gender-Based Violence can be grouped into two broad categories: ________ and ________.
questions.answer: Direct (Physical/Sexual/Psychological) Violence and Structural/Systemic Violence
questions.notes: Includes visible assaults alongside invisible discriminatory laws and cultural deprivations.

questions.question: United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 was adopted in October ________.
questions.notes: Landmark global resolution on Women, Peace and Security (WPS).

questions.question: United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 emphasizes the distinct impact of armed conflict on women and girls, and the necessity of their participation in ________.
questions.answer: Peace negotiations, conflict prevention, peacekeeping, and post-conflict decision-making
questions.notes: Four WPS pillars: Prevention, Participation, Protection, and Relief & Recovery.

questions.question: United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 urges international bodies and member states to integrate gender considerations into ________.
questions.answer: All peacekeeping operations, peace missions, and security sector reform programs
questions.notes: Mandates deployment of gender advisers in international stabilization forces.

questions.question: ________ approaches to GBV as an alternative to punitive legal strategies entail accountability, repair, and community reintegration.
questions.answer: Restorative Justice
questions.notes: Focuses on healing victim harm and transforming community relationships rather than mere retributive punishment.

questions.question: ________ approaches to GBV resolution acknowledge that violence occurs within specific social contexts and advocate that sustainable solutions must engage community structures, norms, and leaders.
questions.answer: Community-Based and Transformative
questions.notes: Involves traditional rulers, religious clergy, and youth assemblies in shifting harmful norms.

questions.question: Write brief notes on the following theoretical perspectives on understanding gender-based violence: (i) Feminist theory, (ii) Social Learning Theory, (iii) Ecological Theory.
questions.answer: (i) Feminist theory: Identifies patriarchal dominance and institutional power imbalances as the root cause of female subordination. (ii) Social Learning Theory: Argues violent behaviour is modeled, observed, and reinforced through socialization in families and peer groups. (iii) Ecological Theory: Analyzes nested interactions across Individual (biology), Relationship (peers/family), Community (schools/neighborhoods), and Societal (laws/cultural norms) spheres.
questions.notes: Comprehensive theoretical grounding for exam essays and continuous assessment.

questions.question: ________ defined health as the state of optimum capacity of an individual for the effective performance of the roles and tasks for which he has been socialized.
questions.answer: Talcott Parsons (1951)
questions.notes: Functionalist sociological perspective framing health as essential for social system stability.

questions.question: ________ conceived health as adaptation to one's physical and social surroundings and having a balance of the two without undue pain, discomfort, or disability.
questions.answer: J. Ralph Audy (1971)
questions.notes: Ecological adaptability definition of health.

questions.question: ________ defined health as a condition of well-being, free of disease or infirmity, and a basic and universal human right.
questions.answer: The World Health Organization (WHO, 1946 Constitution)
questions.notes: 'Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.'

questions.question: What is the major criticism against World Health Organization's (1946) definition of Health?
questions.answer: It is criticized as being overly utopian, idealistic, and unrealistic because achieving 'complete' physical, mental, and social well-being is virtually impossible, inadvertently rendering nearly all humanity permanently 'unhealthy'.
questions.notes: Leaves little room for people living successfully with managed chronic conditions.

questions.question: According to Dolfman (1973), 'health' means ________.
questions.answer: An ability to function adequately in one's environment and adapt to fluctuating stresses
questions.notes: Dynamic equilibrium between human physiology and external stressors.

questions.question: ________ defined disease as a type of internal state, which impairs health by reducing one or more functional abilities of an individual below species-typical levels.
questions.answer: Christopher Boorse (Biostatistical Theory of Disease, 1977)
questions.notes: Defines disease objectively as a biological malfunction.

questions.question: Some pains, sufferings and discomforts which cannot be termed as disease include ________.
questions.answer: Childbirth pains, grief from the bereavement of a loved one, fatigue after rigorous physical labor, and normal biological aging
questions.notes: Natural physiological and emotional experiences distinct from pathological disease.

questions.question: Medical treatment for diseases could be in two forms namely ________ and ________.
questions.answer: Curative (therapeutic) treatment and Preventive (prophylactic) treatment
questions.notes: Eliminating existing pathogens vs vaccinating to avert infection.

questions.question: The use of Statistical normality in explaining disease requires the use of specie's average measurement levels as a yardstick. The indices are ________.
questions.answer: Blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose levels, heart rate, and white blood cell count
questions.notes: Statistical deviations beyond standard standard deviations define clinical abnormality.

questions.question: ________ is a situation when an individual consciously feels that they are unhealthy as a result of pain and discomfort. ________ is a form of medical problem in the human body and system. ________ is a manifestation of such medical problem.
questions.answer: Illness (subjective feeling); Disease (objective biological pathology); Sickness (social role / societal recognition)
questions.notes: The classic sociological triad: Disease (pathology), Illness (subjective experience), Sickness (social status).

questions.question: What are public goods?
questions.answer: Commodities or services provided to all members of a society, typically by the government, that are non-excludable and non-rivalrous in consumption.
questions.notes: Examples include public sanitation, clean air, street lighting, and herd immunity from mass vaccination.

questions.question: Public goods have two main characteristics. Name and briefly explain each: ________ and ________.
questions.answer: (i) Non-excludability: No individual can be effectively excluded from using the good once provided, even if they refuse to pay (free-rider problem). (ii) Non-rivalry: One individual's consumption does not reduce the availability or quality of the good for others.
questions.notes: Core economic criteria distinguishing public goods from private commodities.

questions.question: What are the main distributive factors of public goods in Nigeria?
questions.answer: Political patronage, ethnic considerations, urban-rural disparity, fiscal allocations, and bureaucratic corruption
questions.notes: Skewed distribution leads to severe healthcare marginalization in rural communities.

questions.question: What are the roles government plays in the provision of healthcare? (i), (ii), (iii), (iv).
questions.answer: (i) Direct financing and building of primary, secondary, and tertiary health infrastructure. (ii) Regulatory oversight, standard setting, and drug licensing (via NAFDAC). (iii) Disease surveillance, epidemic outbreak control, and mass immunizations. (iv) Subsidizing essential maternal and child healthcare services.
questions.notes: Sovereign duty under the right to health.

questions.question: Some healthcare issues that require ethical governance in Nigeria are ________.
questions.answer: Equitable access to essential medicines, patient informed consent, clinical trial ethics, brain drain (emigration of doctors/nurses), and end-of-life care
questions.notes: Bioethical challenges in developing healthcare systems.

questions.question: The four principles of ethics in healthcare provision are ________, ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: Autonomy, Beneficence, Non-maleficence, and Justice (Beauchamp & Childress)
questions.notes: Foundational pillar of modern medical bioethics.

questions.question: Why did members of the Hausa-Fulani ethnic group oppose the Federal Government of Nigeria's decision to vaccinate children in a global polio eradication drive in 2003?
questions.answer: Rumors and religious-political suspicions arose that the oral polio vaccines were contaminated with anti-fertility agents and HIV virus by Western powers to depopulate Muslim communities.
questions.notes: Led to an 11-month boycott across Kano, Kaduna, and Zamfara States until independent local testing verified safety.

questions.question: Three examples of the United Nations framework for preventing conflicts in health ethical governance are ________, ________, and ________.
questions.answer: The International Health Regulations (IHR, 2005), the Universal Declaration on Bioethics and Human Rights (UNESCO, 2005), and the UN Guiding Principles on Health in Fragile States
questions.notes: Global governance mechanisms establishing standards during public health emergencies.

questions.question: What is gene therapy?
questions.answer: A medical experimental technique that modifies or alters a person's genes to treat or prevent genetic disorders and hereditary diseases.
questions.notes: Promising clinical advances alongside contentious ethical issues surrounding germline modification and genetic enhancement.

questions.question: What is healthcare delivery conflict?
questions.answer: Disputes, disagreements, and systemic friction arising among healthcare professionals, management, government authorities, and patients regarding resource distribution, wages, working conditions, or clinical negligence.
questions.notes: Frequently manifests in recurrent strikes by medical doctors (NARD) and health workers (JOHESU).

questions.question: What are the possible consequences of healthcare delivery conflicts?
questions.answer: Preventable patient deaths, disruption of emergency medical services, erosion of public trust in healthcare systems, and economic losses.
questions.notes: Paralyzes public hospital operations and exacerbates medical poverty.

questions.question: In what forms can healthcare delivery conflicts manifest? Name and briefly explain each: (i), (ii).
questions.answer: (i) Inter-professional rivalry conflict: Disputes between medical doctors and other allied healthcare professionals (pharmacists, nurses, laboratory scientists) over hospital leadership and salary disparities. (ii) Industrial/Labor disputes: Strike actions between healthcare worker unions and the government over unpaid hazard allowances, dilapidated equipment, and welfare conditions.
questions.notes: Structural friction crippling the Nigerian tertiary health sector.

questions.question: Best (2006) defined ________ as the meticulous examination of any situation utilizing specific frameworks, paradigms, and methodologies.
questions.answer: Conflict Analysis
questions.notes: Diagnostic tool to identify root causes and structural dynamics of disputes.

questions.question: ________ et al. (2000) conceived of conflict analysis as involving the systematic examination and comprehension of the conflict's reality from multiple viewpoints.
questions.answer: Simon Fisher (Responding to Conflict)
questions.notes: Multi-perspectival understanding preventing biased interventions.

questions.question: ________ is a pragmatic instrument that assists conflict managers in efficiently devising their intervention strategies.
questions.answer: Conflict Analysis
questions.notes: Diagnostic foundation for tailored peacebuilding.

questions.question: The three fundamental components of peace practice are: conflict analysis; conflict tracking and ________.
questions.answer: Conflict Evaluation / Impact Assessment (or Peacebuilding Evaluation)
questions.notes: Integrated cycle of intervention design, monitoring, and impact evaluation.

questions.question: The phrase 'Peace Practice' encompasses the full range of peacekeeping, peace-making, and peacebuilding, together referred to as the ________.
questions.answer: Peace Continuum / Peace Architecture
questions.notes: Boutros Boutros-Ghali's Agenda for Peace taxonomy.

questions.question: Conflict tracking employs the systematic methodology known as the ________.
questions.answer: Conflict Early Warning System (CEWS) / Monitoring Matrix
questions.notes: Continuous observation of dynamic conflict indicators.

questions.question: The acronym EWS stands for ________.
questions.answer: Early Warning System
questions.notes: Surveillance framework warning decision-makers of impending violent escalations.

questions.question: ________ represents the final stage in the continuum of peace practice.
questions.answer: Peacebuilding / Post-conflict Reconstruction (Sustainable Peace)
questions.notes: Structural reforms to prevent conflict recurrence.

questions.question: IDASA (2004, p.8) states that 'conflict analysis comprises three stages: pre-conflict analysis, intervention analysis, and ________.'
questions.answer: Post-conflict (or Impact) analysis
questions.notes: Three temporal assessment phases for peace practitioners.

questions.question: The major components of conflict analysis are: Issues, Actors, Conflict Stages, and ________ analysis.
questions.answer: Context (or Structural Dynamics)
questions.notes: The 4 essential dimensions of any comprehensive conflict audit.

questions.question: By ________ in a conflict we refer to individuals or entities who are either directly or indirectly involved in a conflict situation.
questions.answer: Actors (or Stakeholders)
questions.notes: Entities with interests, stakes, or influence in the conflict.

questions.question: Actors in a conflict may also be referred to as ________ or ________.
questions.answer: Stakeholders or Conflict Parties
questions.notes: Entities whose goals are perceived as incompatible.

questions.question: Albert (2001) classified conflict stakeholders into primary, secondary, and ________ Parties.
questions.answer: Tertiary (Shadow / External)
questions.notes: Classification based on directness of involvement.

questions.question: The ________ parties are typically seen as those directly engaged in the conflict.
questions.answer: Primary
questions.notes: Direct antagonists who have direct vested interests in the outcome.

questions.question: The ________ parties are individuals or groups indirectly engaged in the conflict due to their association with the principal parties.
questions.answer: Secondary
questions.notes: Allies, financial sponsors, or sympathizers.

questions.question: The ________ parties are also referred to as allies.
questions.answer: Secondary
questions.notes: Parties lending political, military, or logistic backing.

questions.question: ________ analysis fundamentally involves the examination of a conflict's historical background.
questions.answer: Context (or Historical / Root Cause)
questions.notes: Traces colonial, demographic, and structural grievances over time.

questions.question: The ________ stage of conflict could also be called the formation or latent stage.
questions.answer: Pre-conflict (Latent / Incipient)
questions.notes: Grievances exist beneath the surface without active violence.

questions.question: At the ________ stage of conflict, the parties might engage in some sort of quarrelling as communication begins to be strained.
questions.answer: Confrontation (Escalation)
questions.notes: Polarization worsens and verbal attacks replace constructive engagement.

questions.question: The height or peak of conflict situations is known as the ________ stage.
questions.answer: Crisis (Peak / Climax / Acute)
questions.notes: Open warfare, casualties, and maximum hostility.

questions.question: The ________ stage of conflict explains conflict de-escalation.
questions.answer: De-escalation (Stalemate / Hurting Stalemate / Negotiation)
questions.notes: Parties realize mutually hurting stalemate and seek mediation.

questions.question: What stage of conflict is largely characterized by two levels of activities: improvement and transformation?
questions.answer: Post-conflict (Resolution / Outcome / Transformation)
questions.notes: Rebuilding relationships and reforming underlying social structures.

questions.question: In the onion-doughnut analysis, the outer layer of the onion represents the ________ the actors express publicly.
questions.answer: Positions (what they say they want)
questions.notes: Public posturing masking underlying motives.

questions.question: Also, the onion-doughnut analysis holds that while interests can often be negotiated, ________ are non-negotiable.
questions.answer: Basic Human Needs (identity, security, survival, dignity)
questions.notes: John Burton's Basic Human Needs Theory.

questions.question: The ABC Triangle of conflict analysis is also known as the ________.
questions.answer: Conflict Triangle (Johan Galtung's Model)
questions.notes: Connects Attitude, Behaviour, and Contradiction (Context).

questions.question: The ABC Triangle of conflict analysis was created by peace researcher ________.
questions.answer: Johan Galtung (1969, 1996)
questions.notes: Pioneer of modern peace studies.

questions.question: The ________ method of conflict analysis is best situated in tracking intergroup conflicts.
questions.answer: Conflict Tree (Root, Trunk, Leaves) / Conflict Mapping
questions.notes: Roots: structural causes; Trunk: manifest problem; Leaves: observable effects.

questions.question: The ________ analytical procedure creates two analogous islands extending from the ocean in a pyramidal shape.
questions.answer: Pillars of Conflict / Pyramid Model
questions.notes: Demonstrates structural pillars upholding war or peace systems.

questions.question: A ________ is defined as 'a venue where knowledge is exchanged, and consensus is achieved regarding the nature of the situation, its current state, and its desired future.'
questions.answer: Conflict Analysis Workshop / Dialogue Forum
questions.notes: Facilitated problem-solving session for stakeholders.

questions.question: ________ aim to investigate and ascertain the principal facts pertinent to comprehending a specific conflict or dispute.
questions.answer: Fact-Finding Missions (Inquiries / Commissions)
questions.notes: Neutral investigative teams gathering empirical evidence.

questions.question: What are the paramount tasks in the issue analysis of a conflict?
questions.answer: Identifying the root/underlying causes, immediate triggers, systemic catalysts, and distinguishing tangible issues (land, money) from intangible issues (honor, identity).
questions.notes: Clarifies the core contention points driving the dispute.

questions.question: Briefly explain the following sources for conflict analysis information: (i) Case study, (ii) Analysis Meetings/Workshops, (iii) Fact-finding missions.
questions.answer: (i) Case study: In-depth historical and sociological examination of past similar conflicts to derive insights. (ii) Analysis Workshops: Interactive forums where conflicting parties and experts map dynamics collaboratively. (iii) Fact-finding missions: On-the-ground investigative deployments by independent observers to gather verifiable evidence.
questions.notes: Primary intelligence gathering tools for conflict mediators.

questions.question: Briefly explain the following frameworks for analysis: (i) Onion-Doughnut model, (ii) ABC Triangle.
questions.answer: (i) Onion-Doughnut Model: Peels conflict like an onion through three layers: Outer Layer = Positions (what parties say publicly); Middle Layer = Interests (what they truly want); Core Layer = Needs (fundamental, non-negotiable human requirements for survival, identity, and security). (ii) ABC Triangle: Galtung's model examining: A = Attitudes (prejudices, stereotypes, perceptions); B = Behaviours (threats, verbal attacks, violent coercion); C = Contradiction/Context (the underlying structural dispute or incompatibility of goals).
questions.notes: Foundational diagnostic frameworks taught across peace studies.

questions.question: According to ________, peace education promotes knowledge about the requirements of, the obstacles to, and the possibilities for achieving and maintaining peace.
questions.answer: Betty Reardon (1988)
questions.notes: Pioneering feminist peace educator and scholar.

questions.question: ________ posited that peace education supports the development of skills, capacities, attitudes and values necessary to prevent violence, and to create the conditions conducive to peace, whether at an intrapersonal, interpersonal, intergroup, national or international level.
questions.answer: Ian Harris and John Synott (2002)
questions.notes: Multi-level holistic peace pedagogy.

questions.question: ________ referred to Peace education as a means of ensuring holistic peace in their respective domains.
questions.answer: UNICEF / UNESCO
questions.notes: International mandate for peace education in school curricula.

questions.question: ________ posited that peace education is simply 'teaching about peace' in terms of what it is all about; why it does not (or does) exist; and how to achieve it.
questions.answer: Johan Galtung (1975) / James Page (2008)
questions.notes: Core philosophical query of peace studies.

questions.question: The seven strategies through which teaching and learning about peace suppresses the culture of violence as outlined by the World Health Organization (WHO) are: (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi), (vii).
questions.answer: (i) Developing safe, stable and nurturing relationships between children and parents; (ii) Developing life skills in children and adolescents; (iii) Reducing the availability and misuse of alcohol; (iv) Reducing access to lethal means (guns and weapons); (v) Promoting gender equality to prevent violence against women; (vi) Changing cultural and social norms that support violence; (vii) Victim identification, care and support programmes.
questions.notes: Evidence-based public health strategies to eliminate interpersonal violence.

questions.question: ________ is the peace education directed toward the elimination of violence in all its various forms and manifestations.
questions.answer: Negative Peace Education (Education for Disarmament and Non-violence)
questions.notes: Focuses on stopping direct physical warfare and violent crime.

questions.question: ________ is the nurturing and establishment of the conditions necessary for peace to flourish.
questions.answer: Positive Peace Education (Education for Social Justice, Human Rights, and Structural Equality)
questions.notes: Elimination of structural and cultural violence.

questions.question: ________ and ________ observed that Peace education cultivates the knowledge base, skills, attitudes and values that seek to transform people's mindsets, attitudes and behaviours.
questions.answer: Loreta Castro and Jasmin Galace (2010)
questions.notes: Transformative peace education paradigm.

questions.question: According to UNESCO (2024), the transformative goals of peace education have the following dimensions: ________.
questions.answer: Cognitive (knowledge/critical thinking), Socio-emotional (empathy/tolerance/dialogue), and Behavioural (action for social justice/peacebuilding)
questions.notes: Head, heart, and hand framework of peace education.

questions.question: Briefly elaborate on the transformative goals mentioned above: (i) Cognitive, (ii) Socio-emotional, (iii) Behavioural.
questions.answer: (i) Cognitive: Understanding the roots of conflict, historical injustices, and human rights. (ii) Socio-emotional: Developing deep empathy, emotional self-regulation, compassion, and appreciation of cultural diversity. (iii) Behavioural: Engaging in active non-violent resistance, community dialogue, restorative mediation, and collaborative civic action.
questions.notes: Holistic human development for peaceful coexistence.

questions.question: What is Intrapersonal peace education?
questions.answer: Education that fosters inner peace, emotional self-awareness, mindfulness, psychological balance, and self-acceptance within the individual mind.
questions.notes: Inner harmony prerequisite to peaceful external interactions.

questions.question: What is the relevance of moral education?
questions.answer: It instills ethical values, moral reasoning, social conscience, integrity, and respect for the dignity of every human being, thereby discouraging predatory behaviour and corruption.
questions.notes: Moral compass essential for civic responsibility.

questions.question: What is Interpersonal peace education and what is its scope?
questions.answer: Education focused on constructive communication, conflict handling skills, empathy, active listening, and cooperation in one-on-one and family relationships.
questions.notes: Scope covers resolving peer bullying, marital discord, and neighborly disputes without violence.

questions.question: What are peacebuilding activities in peace education?
questions.answer: Practical experiential initiatives such as peer mediation clubs, inter-ethnic youth camps, community service, peace drama/arts festivals, and grassroots reconciliation workshops.
questions.notes: Translating classroom theory into real community impact.

chapters.chapter_title: Conflict Handling Style and Non-Violent Resistance

questions.question: One of the most significant frameworks for analyzing conflict handling styles was proposed by ________ in 1974.
questions.answer: Kenneth W. Thomas and Ralph H. Kilmann (Thomas-Kilmann Conflict Mode Instrument - TKI)
questions.notes: Maps handling styles along two dimensions: Assertiveness and Cooperativeness.

questions.question: The ________ style is characterized by high assertiveness and low cooperativeness.
questions.answer: Competing (Dominating / Forcing)
questions.notes: Focuses on winning at the other party's expense ('I win, you lose').

questions.question: In assertive and uncooperative situations, the frequent results are ________ outcome.
questions.answer: Win-Lose (Zero-Sum)
questions.notes: One party prevails through power, coercion, or positional rank.

questions.question: In what situations is the competing style often appropriate?
questions.answer: In vital emergencies requiring swift, decisive action; when enforcing unpopular but crucial organizational rules; or when defending against predatory exploitation.
questions.notes: Effective only when speed and decisiveness outweigh relationship building.

questions.question: What are the major disadvantages of the competing style?
questions.answer: It severely damages long-term relationships, provokes deep resentment and retaliation, stifles constructive input, and creates a hostile climate.
questions.notes: High interpersonal costs and post-decision resistance.

questions.question: In ________, individuals are committed to finding solutions that satisfy all parties' concerns. The general result of this scenario is ________ outcome.
questions.answer: Collaborating (Integrating / Problem-Solving); Win-Win (Synergistic)
questions.notes: High assertiveness and high cooperativeness.

questions.question: The collaborating style is most applicable in situations such as ________.
questions.answer: When both parties' concerns are too vital to compromise; when combining diverse perspectives for innovative solutions; and when securing long-term stakeholder commitment.
questions.notes: Best mode for complex, high-stakes organizational issues.

questions.question: The major shortcomings of the collaborating style are that ________.
questions.answer: It demands immense time and energy, requires high trust and transparency, and can lead to analysis paralysis if overused on minor trivial issues.
questions.notes: Resource-intensive conflict mode.

questions.question: The conflict handling style that is moderately assertive and moderately cooperative is ________.
questions.answer: Compromising (Sharing / Negotiating)
questions.notes: Both parties give up something to find an acceptable middle ground.

questions.question: In compromising, mutual concessions mean ________.
questions.answer: Each party splits the difference and surrenders a portion of their goals in exchange for reciprocal concessions ('Give-and-take').
questions.notes: Expedient resolution where neither party gets 100% of their desires.

questions.question: Compromising style is usually suitable in ________.
questions.answer: When goals are moderately important but not worth disruption; when two opponents with equal power are firmly locked in stalemate; or as a temporary settlement under deadline pressure.
questions.notes: Pragmatic intermediate solution.

questions.question: The major shortcoming of the compromising style is that ________.
questions.answer: It may yield sub-optimal, patched-over solutions that fail to address underlying root issues, potentially causing grievances to re-ignite later.
questions.notes: Lose-Lose element where everyone leaves partly dissatisfied.

questions.question: The conflict handling style that is characterized by low assertiveness and low cooperativeness is ________.
questions.answer: Avoiding (Withdrawing / Sidestepping)
questions.notes: Diplomatic withdrawal or postponing action.

questions.question: In conflict handling style, avoidance means ________.
questions.answer: Deliberately ignoring, postponing, or withdrawing from a conflict rather than directly confronting the issues or other parties.
questions.notes: 'I lose, you lose' mode of non-engagement.

questions.question: Avoidance can be strategically effective where ________.
questions.answer: The issue is trivial; emotional tensions are too volatile and cooling-off time is needed; or when others can resolve the conflict more effectively.
questions.notes: Tactical de-escalation pause.

questions.question: What are the major shortcomings of avoidance?
questions.answer: Important problems remain festering and unaddressed; decisions are made by default; and conflict parties experience mounting resentment and frustration.
questions.notes: Chronic avoidance causes explosive future confrontations.

questions.question: ________ is a conflict-handling style in which one person puts the other party's needs, interests, or concerns ahead of their own in order to maintain harmony or preserve a relationship.
questions.answer: Accommodating (Obliging / Smoothing)
questions.notes: Low assertiveness and high cooperativeness ('You win, I lose').

questions.question: The major feature of accommodating is that it essentially prioritizes ________.
questions.answer: Preserving the relationship and communal peace over winning one's personal substantive agenda
questions.notes: Relationship maintenance strategy.

questions.question: What is self-sacrifice in accommodating and what is its major advantage?
questions.answer: Self-sacrifice means willingly conceding one's position to satisfy another; its major advantage is that it restores harmony, builds social capital, and demonstrates goodwill.
questions.notes: Generates reciprocity and de-escalates explosive hostility.

questions.question: What conflict handling style happens when one or both parties refuse to compromise or let go of certain interests but decide to deal decisively with the other party?
questions.answer: Confrontation (Fighting / Coercive Contention)
questions.notes: Escalation into adversarial battle of wills.

questions.question: What is emotional intelligence in conflict handling and explain: (i) Emotions as information, (ii) Emotional arousal and cognitive functioning.
questions.answer: Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize, understand, manage, and constructively influence emotions during disputes. (i) Emotions as information: Emotions signal unmet needs and underlying values. (ii) Emotional arousal and cognitive functioning: Extreme anger or fear triggers amygdala hijack, reducing rational cognitive processing and escalating destructive reactions.
questions.notes: Emotional self-regulation is critical for de-escalating confrontations.

chapters.chapter_title: Peace Psychology: Understanding the Human Mind in Conflict and Reconciliation

questions.question: Peace Psychology evolved as an area of academic study in the second half of the ________.
questions.answer: Twentieth (20th) century (during the Cold War in the 1960s–1980s)
questions.notes: Spurred by existential threats of nuclear confrontation and mass violence.

questions.question: The incidence of peace, conflict, and violence brought together the key practices that define the field of ________.
questions.answer: Peace Psychology
questions.notes: Intersection of psychological science and peace studies.

questions.question: According to Galtung (1969), peace psychology aims to create theories and practices for the prevention and control of ________.
questions.answer: Violence (Direct, Structural, and Cultural violence)
questions.notes: Holistic violence framework of peace research.

questions.question: ________ builds on the concepts of mental processes and behaviour of war and peace.
questions.answer: Peace Psychology
questions.notes: Applies cognitive, emotional, and social psychology to conflict transformation.

questions.question: The tendency of individuals and groups to be involved in violent episodes or its prevention and mitigation is found in their patterns of ________.
questions.answer: Psychological socialization, cognitive schemas, and perceptions of threat/injustice
questions.notes: Human behavior is mediated by internal cognitive and affective filters.

questions.question: According to Eze (2017), ________ is the maintenance of minimal conditions that enable efficient social processes in human society.
questions.answer: Peace (Social Order)
questions.notes: Operational definition of societal stability.

questions.question: A human action that wards off violence and facilitates nonviolent management of conflict is referred to as ________.
questions.answer: Peacemaking / Nonviolent Action
questions.notes: Proactive constructive interventions stopping kinetic aggression.

questions.question: Actions that promote the conditions that ensure social justice and minimize conflict are regarded as ________.
questions.answer: Peacebuilding
questions.notes: Constructing durable structural conditions for long-term equity.

questions.question: According to Christie et al. (2001), peace psychology seeks to develop theories and practices aimed at ________ and mitigating ________ and ________ violence.
questions.answer: preventing; direct (episodic); structural
questions.notes: Standard definition adopted by APA Division 48 (Society for the Study of Peace, Conflict, and Violence).

questions.question: Interpersonal or social conflict is defined as the perception of ________, while ________ refers to coercive actions carried out with the intention of harming others.
questions.answer: incompatible goals or scarce resources; violence
questions.notes: Distinction between conflict (cognitive incompatibility) and violence (harmful behavioral act).

questions.question: What is Episodic violence?
questions.answer: Discrete, acute, and manifest acts of physical harm, assault, armed combat, or riots occurring at a specific time and place.
questions.notes: Direct, visible violence with easily identifiable perpetrators and victims.

questions.question: What is structural violence?
questions.answer: Systemic and institutional mechanisms (poverty, discriminatory laws, caste systems, apartheid) that prevent individuals and groups from meeting their basic needs and realizing their full human potential.
questions.notes: Coined by Johan Galtung: violence built into social structures without an explicit individual assailant.

questions.question: According to the Society for the Study of Peace, Conflict, and Violence (2006), the goals of Peace Psychology are ________.
questions.answer: To understand psychological causes of conflict, apply psychological knowledge to reduce violence, and promote social justice and sustainable peace
questions.notes: Official mandate of APA Division 48.

questions.question: The vision of peace psychologists is ________.
questions.answer: A world where human disputes are addressed through non-violent dialogue, empathy, reconciliation, and structural justice
questions.notes: Transforming adversarial dynamics into collaborative co-existence.

questions.question: Briefly outline the aims of Peace Psychology: (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi).
questions.answer: (i) Analyzing psychological roots of hatred, dehumanization, and intergroup bias. (ii) Mitigating trauma and PTSD in post-war populations. (iii) Fostering intergroup contact and empathy across historical divides. (iv) Promoting non-violent conflict resolution skills in schools and communities. (v) Challenging structural and cultural violence. (vi) Supporting truth, healing, and reconciliation processes.
questions.notes: Comprehensive clinical and social peace psychology agenda.

questions.question: Who proposed the concepts of positive peace and negative peace?
questions.answer: Johan Galtung (1964, 1969)
questions.notes: Foundational dichotomy of international peace research.

questions.question: What is positive peace?
questions.answer: The presence of social justice, equality, institutional fairness, human rights, and the total absence of both direct and structural violence.
questions.notes: Sustainable flourishing of society.

questions.question: What is negative peace?
questions.answer: The mere absence of direct, active physical violence or war, even while underlying injustices, oppression, and fear persist.
questions.notes: Unstable ceasefires without systemic justice.

chapters.chapter_title: Legal Framework for Social Justice and Conflict Resolution in Nigeria

questions.question: The major legal instrument for the defence of human rights in Nigeria derives from the ________.
questions.answer: 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (Chapter IV: Fundamental Rights)
questions.notes: Sections 33 to 44 guarantee fundamental human rights (Right to life, dignity, personal liberty, fair hearing, etc.).

questions.question: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights to which Nigeria is a signatory is an example of a ________.
questions.answer: Multilateral International Human Rights Treaty / Global Normative Instrument
questions.notes: Adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948.

questions.question: ________ establishes the legal framework and other mechanisms to hold government accountable in the event they violate human rights.
questions.answer: Constitutionalism (The Rule of Law and Judicial Review)
questions.notes: Limits arbitrary government power through independent courts.

questions.question: Legal framework can be viewed from ________ and ________ dimensions.
questions.answer: Substantive (statutory laws, rights, doctrines) and Procedural / Institutional (courts, enforcement agencies, rules of litigation)
questions.notes: Two interdependent pillars of any jurisprudence system.

questions.question: ________ provides a basis for enforcing law and policies that promote order, justice and fairness.
questions.answer: The Legal Framework / The Constitution
questions.notes: Supreme law of the land from which all institutional legitimacy derives (Section 1(1) & 1(3)).

questions.question: Legal framework can best be conceptualized as ________.
questions.answer: A coherent system of interrelated laws, judicial precedents, constitutional principles, and regulatory institutions that govern societal behavior and arbitrate disputes
questions.notes: The bedrock of modern democratic governance.

questions.question: According to FasterCapital (2024), a legal framework provides ________.
questions.answer: Legal predictability, contractual certainty, protection of property rights, and institutional checks and balances
questions.notes: Essential for conflict resolution and socio-economic investment.

questions.question: The growth of Nigeria's legal system has been linked to ________.
questions.answer: English Common Law tradition, Islamic (Sharia) Law, and Indigenous Customary Law (the tripartite legal heritage)
questions.notes: Pluralistic nature of Nigerian jurisprudence.

questions.question: Human rights issues have been a subject for debate in ________ and ________ circles since the ________ and ________ until the present democratic government.
questions.answer: academic and civil society / political; colonial era and military regimes
questions.notes: Long struggles against authoritarian decrees to achieve constitutional democracy.

chapters.chapter_title: Community Policing: Evolution and Imperatives for Conflict Resolution

questions.question: Community policing differs significantly from conventional policing approaches that stress coercive authority, ________, and ________.
